query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, surface-deposited alumina-rich (Al2O3) coating to refractory high-entropy alloys will significantly improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a continuous, slow-growing barrier that limits oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) in its as-cast or conventionally processed state that typically forms non-protective oxide scales under oxidative high-temperature conditions.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin, dense Al2O3-rich coating (using techniques such as chemical vapor deposition or physical vapor deposition) on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Expose the coated alloy to air at approximately 1100°C for up to 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The preformed, continuous alumina scale created by the coating acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: The Al2O3 coating forms a stable, adherent, and slow-growing protective layer at high temperatures that prevents or delays oxygen ingress into the underlying RHEA, reducing the formation of deleterious oxide phases that compromise mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the specified conditions, the coated RHEA will exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate, for example, a reduction in oxidation weight gain of at least 50% relative to an untreated control alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated RHEA specimens which, when exposed to 1100°C in air, develop thicker, less protective oxide scales resulting in higher oxidation weight gains and potential degradation of mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to be most pronounced under high-temperature oxidative conditions (around 1100°C in air); the performance might vary if exposure times are substantially extended or if the oxygen partial pressure differs significantly from atmospheric levels.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the long-term adhesion and integrity of the Al2O3 coating under thermal cycling, and the exact magnitude of oxidation resistance improvement could depend on the coating process details and alloy-specific interactions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same batch of RHEA: one set with the applied Al2O3-rich coating and one untreated set. Subject both sets to oxidation testing by exposing them to air at 1100°C for 100 hours. After exposure, measure the oxidation weight gain, examine the surface oxide morphology, and evaluate the continuity and thickness of the oxide layers using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX).
measurements: Oxidation weight gain per unit area
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via cross-sectional SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit at least a 50% reduction in oxidation weight gain (or show no statistically significant improvement in oxide scale quality compared to the untreated samples) under the conditions tested, the hypothesis is falsified.
